content:
"The passage critiques the enduring appeal of the “great men” theory of history, a 19th-century idea associated with the belief that exceptional individuals shape world events through their talent, courage, charisma, genius and force of personality. Although later intellectual movements, including egalitarian thought, Marxist social theory and the “history from below” approach linked to EP Thompson, challenged this top-down view of the past, the article argues that the idea has remained surprisingly persistent.

The piece refers to the Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, who treated figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther and the prophet Muhammad as extraordinary heroes whose actions permanently transformed history. In Carlyle’s view, ordinary people were largely passive observers, destined to admire and follow these dominant figures who supposedly made “universal history” from above.

However, the article strongly questions this belief, calling it foolish yet seductive. It suggests that even today, some powerful individuals, mostly men, still imagine themselves as heroic figures chosen for a special mission. They see themselves as uniquely wise, called to lead, rescue nations or peoples, and impose their vision on others. These self-styled saviours believe they understand the world better than everyone else and often possess the arrogance and ruthlessness needed to force their ideas into reality.

The passage concludes by emphasizing that in the modern era such “great” men are usually not heroes in any ordinary moral sense. Rather than noble leaders, they are more often anti-heroes or villains who, like Carlyle’s historical figures, hold significant power but use it in troubling and dangerous ways."
